title: Exploiting Similarities in A/B Testing with Off-Policy Estimation

problem.claim: A/B testing measures the performance gain of a new decision system relative to a baseline.

gap.claim: Traditional A/B testing treats systems as black boxes and ignores similarities between them, making the commonly used difference-in-means estimator statistically suboptimal when similarities exist.

contributions.claim: Introduces a family of A/B testing estimators that use tested systems' decision propensities through off-policy estimation.
The estimator family can be tailored to practical decision-making.
Provides theoretical analysis of the proposed estimators' efficiency and practicality.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The resulting estimators have improved concentration properties.
The estimators are reported to be simple, robust to propensity misspecification, and substantially more accurate when tested systems exhibit similarities.
Theoretical analysis and empirical studies are reported to confirm the estimators' efficiency and practicality.

narrative_sequence.summary: Defines A/B testing as a protocol for comparing a new decision system with a baseline.
Identifies that conventional black-box treatment ignores structural similarities that commonly exist between systems.
States that difference-in-means is statistically suboptimal when such similarities are present.
Introduces flexible off-policy estimators that exploit system propensities.
Reports improved accuracy and robustness, fallback to difference-in-means without similarities, and support from theoretical and empirical studies.

source_observation.claim: The proposed estimators exploit similarities between systems through their propensities and fall back to difference-in-means when similarities are absent.

interpretation.claim: Using shared structure can improve estimation while preserving a conventional baseline behavior when the structure is unavailable.

application.claim: In comparative evaluation, incorporate measurable similarities between systems into estimators while retaining a fallback estimator for dissimilar cases.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the conditions, thresholds, or failure modes governing the fallback behavior.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the estimator formulas or theoretical assumptions.
The abstract does not report datasets, experimental settings, numerical results, or comparison baselines beyond difference-in-means.
The abstract does not define how propensity similarity is measured or how misspecification is handled.
